readerTitle: When every team wins and the company loses
caseNote: 가상 사례 2개 (가구 공장, 철물 유통업체) + 가상 적용 (가계부 앱) · 수치 없이 설명
insight: 한 부서의 개선은 그 부서의 숫자가 아니라 회사 전체가 내는 결과로 판단해야 하며, 개선을 축하하기 전에 그 비용이 어느 부서로 넘어갔는지 물어야 한다.
misconception: 모든 부서가 각자 목표를 최대로 달성하면 회사 전체 성과도 최대가 된다.

sources.text: Goldratt, E. M. & Cox, J. (1984). The Goal: A Process of Ongoing Improvement. North River Press.
Deming, W. E. (1993). The New Economics for Industry, Government, Education. MIT. (부분 최적화, suboptimization 논의)
공장, 유통업체, 앱 사례는 모두 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 6번 카드 callout: 『The Goal』이 1984년에 처음 출간된 비즈니스 소설이며 병목(bottleneck)이 공장 전체의 산출 속도를 정한다는 내용이 핵심이라는 점을 게시 전에 확인하세요.
5번 카드의 'suboptimization' 용어는 시스템 사고와 Deming의 저술에서 쓰이는 일반 용어입니다. 카드에서는 특정 인물의 발언으로 인용하지 않았습니다. 출처 표기가 정확한지 확인하세요.
모든 사례는 가상이며 구체적 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다. '배치 4배' 외에 계산이 필요한 숫자는 없습니다.

cards.title: When every team wins and the company loses
body: A furniture factory's cutting department just posted its lowest cost per part ever. Across town, a hardware distributor's buyer just landed the best supplier prices in years.
Both managers expect praise. Both companies had a worse quarter than the one before. The reason is the same.

image.label: Two managers holding trophies in front of struggling businesses
image.brief: 화면을 좌우로 나눔. 왼쪽은 가구 공장 재단 부서 관리자가 트로피를 들고 웃고, 뒤로 재단된 목재 더미가 통로를 막고 있음. 오른쪽은 유통업체 구매 담당자가 트로피를 들고, 뒤 창고에 같은 상자가 천장까지 쌓임. 두 장면 위에 하락하는 회사 전체 그래프를 작게. 실제 로고·상표 없음.

cards.title: Bigger batches, cheaper parts?
body: You run a furniture factory. Wood is cut, then sanded and finished, then packed. Every time cutting switches to a new design, its machines stop for an hour of setup.
The cutting manager wants to cut each design in batches four times larger. Fewer setups, lower cost per cut part. What do you say?

options.text: Approve it. Lower cost per part means lower cost overall
options.feedback: It sounds like pure savings. But customers don't buy cut parts, and if finishing can't keep up, the extra parts just wait while orders for other designs wait longer.

options.text: First check what it does to finished orders shipped on time
options.feedback: This judges the change by the result the whole factory exists for. It may still be a good idea, but only if the later steps can use what cutting makes.

options.text: Approve it for a month and track cutting's cost per part
options.feedback: A short, reversible trial is sensible. But tracking only cutting's cost will show success even if the factory as a whole gets slower.

cards.title: The factory got cheaper and slower.
body: The factory approved the bigger batches. Cutting's cost per part fell, just as promised.

But finishing could only handle so much each day. Stacks of cut parts filled the aisles, and workers hunted for the right pieces. A customer ordering a less popular design now waited weeks, because cutting was busy with a huge run of something else.
Cutting's numbers improved. Shipped orders, cash and customer patience got worse.

cards.title: The distributor got cheaper and poorer.
body: At the hardware distributor, the buyer is judged on purchase price. Suppliers give the best price for full truckloads, so the buyer orders full truckloads.

Unit costs dropped. But the warehouse filled with a year's supply of slow sellers. Cash was tied up in boxes, so fast sellers ran short. Months later, the extra stock was sold off at a discount that erased the savings.

image.label: A warehouse overflowing with one product while another shelf is empty
image.brief: 창고 내부. 왼쪽 선반은 같은 상자(예: 페인트 통)가 넘칠 만큼 쌓여 있고 'Slow seller' 라벨. 오른쪽 선반은 비어 있고 'Out of stock' 표지. 바닥에 'Clearance' 할인 스티커가 붙은 상자들. 실제 브랜드·로고 없음.

cards.title: Local wins, global losses
body: A **local win** improves one part of a business by that part's own measure. A **global loss** is what happens when that win makes the whole business worse.
Systems thinkers call this *suboptimization*: improving a part at the expense of the whole. Nobody in either story was careless. Each manager did exactly what their own numbers rewarded.

image.label: One gear spinning fast while the connected machine jams
image.brief: 맞물린 톱니바퀴 여러 개로 된 기계 인포그래픽. 한 톱니만 빛나며 빠르게 돌고 '+ Local win' 표시, 그 옆 톱니 사이에 부품이 끼어 기계 전체 출력 화살표가 줄어들며 '− Global loss' 표시. 단순한 플랫 스타일.

cards.title: Why it keeps happening.
body: Local wins turn into global losses for a few common reasons:
list: **Costs land elsewhere:** cutting saved setup time, while finishing and sales paid in delays
**Each team sees its own numbers:** the buyer saw unit price, not storage, cash or markdowns
**A chain moves at its slowest step:** speeding up any other step just builds a pile in front of it
cards.callout: Eliyahu Goldratt built his 1984 business novel *The Goal* around that last point: a factory makes money only as fast as its bottleneck works.

cards.title: Don't throw out local goals.
body: Teams need their own measures. Nobody can steer by company profit alone every day, and many local improvements really do help the whole.

The fix is a habit, not a ban. Before celebrating a team's win, ask where its costs went. Pair each local measure with one shared result, such as orders shipped on time or cash tied up in stock. A whole-system check takes time, so save it for changes that touch other teams.

cards.title: Now it's an app.
body: You lead a budgeting app. Three product teams each own a feature and are measured on how many users try it. Each team has added a pop-up nudging users toward its feature.
Every team's numbers are up. Overall, more users are turning off notifications and leaving. What do you change?

options.text: Test each pop-up on its own and keep the ones that lift their feature
options.feedback: Testing is good discipline, but each test measures a local win. Every pop-up can pass its own test while the pile of them drives users away.

options.text: Cap pop-ups across the app and give one owner a goal tied to users staying
options.feedback: Each team loses some reach for its feature. In return, someone weighs every nudge against the whole experience users actually feel.

options.text: Keep going. Three teams hitting their goals is a good sign
options.feedback: Each team wins on paper. The users who leave are a cost that no team's dashboard shows.

cards.title: Before you celebrate a team's win, find where its costs went.
body: One part of a business can get better while the whole gets worse. Judge a change by what the whole business delivers, not by the number of the team that made it.
**Try it today:** pick one team's main metric. Ask which other team pays when that number improves.
